sentences.text: The skull of this creature featured a pointed snout and a large, horizontally oriented nostril.
Oblique grooves in the jaw joints allowed the animal to widen its mouth gape when opening its lower jaws.
A shallow depression pierced by a smaller foramen is present in the corner of the lacrimal bone.
The ilium features a 'brevis shelf' formed by the rear blade, which functions as an attachment area for the tail muscle Musculus caudofemoralis brevis.
Eustreptospondylus was a bipedal carnivore with a slender tail, powerful hind legs, an erect posture, and small arms.
Unlike Megalosaurus, Eustreptospondylus had a thinner and more slender physical build.
Eustreptospondylus remains the most complete large Jurassic theropod found in Europe.
The holotype specimen was a subadult individual estimated to be about 4.63 meters long and weighing about 218 kilograms.
The holotype skeleton of Eustreptospondylus was discovered in 1870 at the Summertown Brick Pit near Oxford, England.
John Phillips described the Eustreptospondylus bones in 1871 without assigning a name at that time.
Alick Donald Walker established the genus and species Eustreptospondylus oxoniensis in 1964.
Like many other theropods, this animal consumed smaller dinosaurs and pterosaurs or scavenged carcasses of fish, marine reptiles, and other dinosaurs.
Because fossils were found on islands when Europe was an archipelago, Eustreptospondylus might have been capable of swimming short distances.
The hypothesis that Eustreptospondylus evolved insular dwarfism is debated, as some researchers argue the small size was due to the holotype being a subadult.
Eustreptospondylus is commonly classified as a member of the Eustreptospondylinae clade within the Megalosauridae.
In 2003, Rauhut proposed that Eustreptospondylus oxoniensis should be classified as Magnosaurus oxoniensis.
In 2010, Gregory S. Paul considered Eustreptospondylus oxoniensis identical to Streptospondylus altdorfensis.
The holotype specimen was recovered from the Callovian stage of the Oxford Clay Formation approximately 162 million years ago.
Eustreptospondylus lived during the Middle Jurassic, approximately 164 to 161 million years ago, in the Callovian stage of what is now Europe.
It is debated whether Eustreptospondylus was a swimmer or if its fossils were transported to the sea by floods or rivers after death.
In 2000, researchers David Martill and Darren Naish argued that the animal was incorrectly described as an island dwarf because the holotype was actually a subadult.
